docs.title: Why Do We Need Computer Networks?
Big Question
docs.text:
How do billions of digital devices communicate and share information every second?

Modern life depends on computer networks. Whether you send a message, watch a video, print homework, or play an online game, a network is working behind the scenes.

In this lesson, you will discover how networks connect people and devices around the world.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Explain why computer networks are important.
  • Describe the benefits of connecting computers.
  • Compare a Local Area Network (LAN) and a Wide Area Network (WAN).
  • Identify common networking devices.
  • Draw a simple network diagram.
  • Explain how schools use computer networks every day.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
You are successful if you can:

✅ Explain what a computer network is.

✅ Give examples of LANs and WANs.

✅ Identify the role of a router and a switch.

✅ Design a simple classroom network.

So how did all of these systems communicate?

The answer is computer networks.

docs.title: What Is a Computer Network?
docs.text:
Definition

A computer network is a group of two or more digital devices connected together so they can communicate and share information.

Networks may be very small or extremely large.

For example,

  • two computers connected by a cable
  • every computer inside a school
  • millions of computers connected through the Internet

are all examples of networks.

The main purpose of a network is sharing.

Computers share:

  • information
  • printers
  • Internet connections
  • files
  • software
  • cloud storage
  • communication services

Without networks, every computer would work completely alone.

docs.title: Why Are Networks Important?
docs.text:
Imagine a school with 600 students.

Without a network,

  • every student needs a separate printer.
  • every teacher copies files using USB drives.
  • homework cannot be submitted online.
  • classroom presentations cannot be shared instantly.
  • there is no Internet access.

Clearly, this would waste time, money, and resources.

Networks solve these problems.

docs.title: 1. Resource Sharing
docs.text:
Many users can use the same printer, scanner, or Internet connection.

Example:

Twenty students can print using one shared network printer.

docs.title: 2. File Sharing
docs.text:
Students can submit homework electronically.

Teachers can distribute worksheets instantly.

Cloud services such as Google Drive work because computers are connected through networks.

docs.title: 3. Communication
docs.text:
Networks allow people to communicate quickly using:

  • Email
  • Video calls
  • Instant messaging
  • Online learning platforms

Modern education depends heavily on network communication.

docs.title: 4. Collaboration
docs.text:
Groups can work on the same document at the same time.

For example,

four students may edit the same presentation simultaneously.

Without networks, collaboration would be much slower.

docs.title: Types of Computer Networks
docs.text:
Not all computer networks are the same.

Some networks connect only a few devices inside a room, while others connect billions of devices around the world.

The size and purpose of a network determine its type.

The two most common types of networks are:

  • Local Area Network (LAN)
  • Wide Area Network (WAN)

docs.title: Local Area Network (LAN)
docs.text:
Definition

A Local Area Network (LAN) is a network that connects devices within a limited geographical area.

Examples include:

  • a classroom
  • a school
  • a home
  • an office

A LAN is usually owned and managed by one person or one organisation.

docs.title: Characteristics of a LAN
docs.text:
• Covers a small area
  • High data transfer speed
  • More secure than public networks
  • Easy to maintain
  • Usually uses Ethernet cables or Wi-Fi

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Your school network is a LAN.

All student laptops, teachers' computers, printers, interactive displays and servers are connected together inside the school.

docs.title: Wide Area Network (WAN)
docs.text:
Definition

A Wide Area Network (WAN) connects multiple LANs across large geographical distances.

Unlike a LAN, a WAN may connect cities, countries or even continents.

The best-known example of a WAN is the Internet.

Other examples include:

  • a company with offices in different countries
  • a bank connecting hundreds of branches
  • an international school group sharing one system

docs.title: Characteristics of a WAN
docs.text:
• Covers a large geographical area
  • Connects many LANs
  • Usually slower than a LAN
  • Often uses public communication infrastructure
  • More expensive to build and maintain

docs.title: Network Devices
docs.text:
Computer networks require special hardware to send data efficiently.

Each device has a different responsibility.

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
Router

A router connects different networks together.

A router decides where data should travel.

For example,

When you open a website,

Laptop

→ School Router

→ Internet

→ Website Server

→ School Router

→ Laptop

Without a router, your school network could not communicate with the Internet.

docs.title: Switch
docs.text:
Switch

A switch connects devices inside the same LAN.

Imagine your classroom has:

  • 30 laptops
  • 1 printer
  • 1 teacher computer

The switch allows every device to communicate efficiently without sending data to every computer.

Think of a switch as a traffic controller inside your school.

docs.title: Wireless Access Point (WAP)
docs.text:
A Wireless Access Point allows wireless devices to connect to the network.

Examples include:

  • laptops
  • tablets
  • smartphones

Without a WAP, wireless devices could not join the school network.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
A server provides services or resources to other computers.

Examples include:

  • File server
  • Print server
  • Web server
  • Authentication server

Many users can access one server at the same time.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
A client is a device that requests information or services from a server.

Examples include:

  • your laptop
  • your tablet
  • your smartphone

Whenever you open Google Classroom, your laptop acts as a client.

Every day, billions of messages, photos, videos and emails travel through routers and switches around the world.

Although most people never see these devices, modern society depends on them every second.

docs.title: How Does Data Travel Through a Network?
docs.text:
When you send a message to a friend or open a website, the information does not travel as one large block of data.

Instead, the data is divided into many small pieces called packets.

Each packet travels independently through the network and may even take a different route to reach its destination.

When all the packets arrive, the receiving device puts them back together in the correct order.

What is a Packet?

A packet is a small unit of data sent across a computer network. Each packet contains part of the message, along with information about where it came from and where it should go.

This method makes communication faster, more reliable, and more efficient.

docs.title: Imagine This
docs.text:
Suppose you want to send a 500-page book to a friend.

Instead of placing the whole book into one enormous box, you divide it into 500 numbered envelopes.

Each envelope can travel separately through the postal system.

Even if one envelope is delayed, the others can continue their journey.

When your friend receives all the envelopes, they simply arrange them in order to rebuild the book.

Network packets work in a very similar way.

docs.title: Why Do Networks Use Packets?
docs.text: Using packets provides several advantages.

docs.title: Faster Transmission
docs.text: Different packets can travel along different routes at the same time.

docs.title: Better Reliability
docs.text:
If one packet is lost, only that packet needs to be sent again.

The entire message does not need to be retransmitted.

docs.title: Efficient Use of the Network
docs.text: Many users can share the same network without one large file blocking everyone else.

docs.title: Lesson 2 – How Does the Internet Work?
Learning Intentions
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will learn:

  • how computers communicate across the Internet.
  • the difference between a client and a server.
  • why every device needs an IP address.
  • why humans use domain names instead of numbers.
  • how the Domain Name System (DNS) works.
  • the journey of a webpage from a web server to your browser.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, I can:

☐ explain the client–server model.

☐ identify the purpose of an IP address.

☐ explain why DNS is important.

☐ describe the steps that occur when loading a webpage.

☐ use networking vocabulary correctly.

docs.title: Think About It
docs.text:
Imagine you type the following address into your web browser.

www.wikipedia.org

Within a second, the webpage appears.

Have you ever wondered what happens during that short time?

Discuss the following questions with a partner.

  1. How does your computer know where Wikipedia is?
  2. How does the webpage travel to your computer?
  3. Why does it happen so quickly?

Write down your ideas.

Remember:

There are no wrong answers at this stage. Today's lesson will help you discover what really happens.

docs.title: Lesson Overview
docs.text:
Every day you:

  • search Google
  • watch YouTube
  • send messages
  • play online games
  • submit homework

Although these tasks seem simple, they require thousands of computers around the world to communicate with each other.

The Internet is not a single computer.

Instead, it is a massive network made up of millions of connected devices.

Every webpage, photograph, video, email and online game relies on computers sending information to one another.

To understand how this works, we first need to learn about clients and servers.

docs.title: Clients and Servers
docs.text:
Imagine walking into a restaurant.

You ask for food.

The kitchen prepares the meal.

Finally, the waiter brings the food to your table.

A computer network works in a similar way.

One computer asks for information.

Another computer provides the information.

These two roles are called the client and the server.

docs.title: What Is a Client?
docs.text:
A client is a device that requests information or services.

Examples include:

  • desktop computers
  • laptops
  • smartphones
  • tablets
  • smart TVs
  • game consoles

Whenever you open a webpage or watch a video, your device is acting as a client.

docs.title: What Is a Server?
docs.text:
A server is a computer that provides information or services to clients.

Servers are usually much more powerful than personal computers because they may serve thousands or even millions of users at the same time.

Examples include:

  • school learning management systems
  • Google Drive
  • Microsoft OneDrive
  • YouTube
  • Netflix
  • online game servers

docs.title: Client or Server?
docs.text:
Decide whether each device is acting as a client or a server.

Situation Client Server Watching YouTube on a phone □ □ Opening a school website □ □ Printing a document through the school print server □ □ Downloading homework from Google Classroom □ □

docs.title: The Client–Server Model
docs.text:
The client–server model describes how computers communicate across a network.

The process is simple.

Step 1

The client sends a request.

Step 2

The server receives the request.

Step 3

The server processes the request.

Step 4

The server sends a response.

Step 5

The client displays the result.

Insert Figure: docs/assets/images/grade9/unit3/client-server.svg

Figure 2.1. The client–server model. A client requests information, and a server responds.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose you visit:

www.bbc.com

Your laptop sends a request asking for the BBC homepage.

The BBC web server receives the request, finds the webpage files, and sends them back across the Internet.

Your browser receives the response and displays the webpage.

This entire process usually takes less than one second.

docs.title: Activity 1 – Acting It Out
docs.text:
Work in groups of three.

Assign the following roles:

  • Student A: Client
  • Student B: Server
  • Student C: Network

Use a sheet of paper as the "request."

  1. The client writes a request.
  2. The network carries the request.
  3. The server writes a response.
  4. The network delivers the response.
  5. The client reads the response.

After the activity, discuss:

  • Which role was responsible for asking for information?
  • Which role stored the information?
  • Why is the network important?

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
Answer the following questions.

  1. What is the main role of a client?
  1. What is the main role of a server?
  1. What is the difference between a request and a response?
  1. Give one example of a client that you use every day.

docs.title: Did You Know?
docs.text:
Some of the world's largest companies operate millions of servers.

These servers are located in data centres around the world and work together to provide websites, cloud storage, online games and streaming services to billions of users every day.

This is why popular websites remain available even when millions of people visit them at the same time.

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: Word Definition Client A device that requests information. Server A computer that provides information or services. Request A message asking for information. Response Information returned by a server. Client–Server Model A way computers communicate by requesting and providing services.

docs.title: Coming Next
docs.text:
Now that you understand how computers communicate, the next question is:

How does the Internet know which computer should receive the information?

docs.title: To answer that, we need to learn about IP addresses.
IP Addresses – Every Device Needs an Address
docs.text:
Imagine that your friend wants to send you a birthday card.

If the envelope has no address, the post office will not know where to deliver it.

The Internet works in a similar way.

Every device connected to a network must have an address so that data knows where to go.

This address is called an Internet Protocol (IP) address.

An IP address is a unique numerical identifier assigned to a device on a network.

Without IP addresses, computers would not know where to send or receive information.

Insert Figure: docs/assets/images/grade9/unit3/ip-address.svg

Figure 2.2. Every device on a network requires a unique IP address.

docs.title: An Example of an IPv4 Address
docs.text:
An IPv4 address consists of four numbers separated by periods.

192.168.1.15

Each number ranges from 0 to 255.

Examples include:

10.0.0.25

172.16.5.100

203.15.88.9

These numbers may not be easy for people to remember, but computers can process them quickly.

docs.title: Public and Private IP Addresses
docs.text:
Not every IP address is visible on the Internet.

There are two common types.

docs.title: Public IP Address
docs.text:
A public IP address is visible on the Internet.

It allows your home or school network to communicate with websites and online services around the world.

Your Internet Service Provider (ISP) usually assigns this address.

docs.title: Private IP Address
docs.text:
A private IP address is used only inside a local network.

Examples include devices connected to your home Wi-Fi or your school's network.

Private IP addresses cannot normally be accessed directly from the Internet.

docs.title: Check Your Understanding
docs.text:
Which type of IP address is most likely used by the following?

Device Public Private Your laptop at school □ □ Your home router □ □ A classroom printer □ □ A school desktop computer □ □

Discuss your answers with a partner.

docs.title: IPv4 and IPv6
docs.text:
When the Internet was first developed, engineers believed there would be enough IPv4 addresses for everyone.

Today, billions of devices are connected to the Internet.

This includes:

  • computers
  • smartphones
  • tablets
  • smart watches
  • smart TVs
  • game consoles
  • security cameras
  • Internet of Things (IoT) devices

Because so many devices now require addresses, a newer system was introduced.

This system is called IPv6.

docs.title: Comparing IPv4 and IPv6
docs.text:
IPv4 IPv6 Older system Newer system Four groups of numbers Eight groups of hexadecimal values About 4.3 billion addresses An extremely large number of addresses Still widely used Increasingly common

You do not need to memorise IPv6 addresses.

Instead, remember why IPv6 was developed.

It provides enough addresses for the future growth of the Internet.

docs.title: Did You Know?
docs.text:
If every person on Earth owned several Internet-connected devices, IPv4 would not provide enough unique addresses.

IPv6 was designed to solve this problem.

docs.title: Domain Names
docs.text:
Imagine trying to remember the following number.

142.250.190.78

Most people would quickly forget it.

Now compare it with:

www.google.com

Which one is easier to remember?

Most people prefer names instead of numbers.

A domain name is a human-readable name that represents an IP address.

Some examples include:

  • www.google.com
  • www.wikipedia.org
  • www.bbc.com
  • www.openai.com

When you type a domain name into your browser, your computer still needs the IP address.

Something must translate the name into the correct number.

That is the job of DNS.

Insert Figure: docs/assets/images/grade9/unit3/url-breakdown.svg

Figure 2.3. A web address contains several parts that help identify a website.

docs.title: The Domain Name System (DNS)
docs.text:
DNS stands for Domain Name System.

DNS is often described as the phone book of the Internet.

Imagine that you want to call a friend.

You probably search for their name in your contacts instead of memorising their phone number.

DNS performs a similar task.

It looks up the IP address that matches a domain name.

docs.title: How DNS Works
docs.text:
Suppose you type:

www.wikipedia.org

The following steps occur.

  1. Your browser sends a request.
  2. The request reaches a DNS server.
  3. The DNS server finds the correct IP address.
  4. The IP address is returned to your browser.
  5. Your browser contacts the correct web server.

All of this usually happens in less than a second.

Insert Figure: docs/assets/images/grade9/unit3/dns-process.svg

Figure 2.4. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses before communication begins.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text: Let's follow the journey of a website request.

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
You type:

www.nasa.gov

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Your browser asks a DNS server:

"What is the IP address for www.nasa.gov?"

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text: The DNS server returns the correct IP address.

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text: Your browser sends a request to NASA's web server.

docs.title: Step 5
docs.text: The server sends the webpage back to your computer.

docs.title: Step 6
docs.text:
Your browser displays the webpage.

Although this process involves multiple computers around the world, it normally takes less than a second.

docs.text:

docs.title: Key Ideas So Far
docs.text:
You should now understand that:

  • every device requires an IP address.
  • domain names are easier for humans to remember than numbers.
  • DNS translates names into IP addresses.
  • clients communicate with servers using IP addresses.
  • the Internet depends on many systems working together.

docs.title: Coming Next
docs.text:
You now know how computers find one another.

The next question is:

docs.title: How does an entire webpage travel across the Internet and appear in your browser?
How a Web Page Loads
docs.text:
When you open a website, many different systems work together to display the page on your screen.

Although this process seems almost instant, several important steps happen behind the scenes.

Understanding these steps helps us understand how the Internet works.

docs.title: Step 1 – Enter a URL
docs.text:
The process begins when you type a web address, also called a URL (Uniform Resource Locator), into your browser.

For example:

https://www.wikipedia.org

The browser first checks whether it already knows the IP address of the website. If it does not, it asks a DNS server for help.

docs.title: Step 2 – DNS Finds the IP Address
docs.text:
The DNS server searches its records and returns the correct IP address.

Your browser now knows exactly which web server it needs to contact.

Without DNS, you would need to type long numerical IP addresses instead of easy-to-remember website names.

docs.title: Step 3 – The Browser Sends a Request
docs.text:
The browser sends a request across the Internet to the web server.

This request asks for the webpage and any resources needed to display it, such as images, style sheets and scripts.

docs.title: Step 4 – The Server Responds
docs.text:
The web server processes the request.

It locates the required files and sends them back to your browser.

This response may include:

  • HTML files
  • CSS files
  • JavaScript files
  • Images
  • Videos
  • Fonts

docs.title: Step 5 – The Browser Builds the Page
docs.text:
Your browser receives the files and combines them to create the webpage you see.

Although these steps involve many computers and networks around the world, they usually take less than one second.

Insert Figure: docs/assets/images/grade9/unit3/how-web-page-loads.svg

Figure 2.5. The journey of a webpage from the browser to the server and back again.

docs.title: Data Travels in Packets
docs.text:
Earlier, you learned that networks send information using packets.

A packet is a small piece of data.

Instead of sending one very large file all at once, the file is divided into many smaller packets.

Each packet may travel along a different route through the Internet.

When the packets arrive at your computer, they are placed back into the correct order.

This process is usually so fast that users never notice it happening.

Insert Figure: docs/assets/images/grade9/unit3/packet-transmission.svg

Figure 2.6. Data is divided into packets before travelling across the network.

docs.title: Why Use Packets?
docs.text:
Sending information as packets has several advantages.

  • Packets can take different routes if one path is busy.
  • Lost packets can be sent again without resending the entire file.
  • Many users can share the same network efficiently.
  • Large files can be transferred more reliably.

docs.title: Case Study – Opening a School Learning Portal
docs.text:
Imagine that you want to access your school's Learning Management System (LMS).

The following events take place.

  1. You enter the school's website address.
  2. DNS finds the correct IP address.
  3. Your browser sends a request.
  4. The school server receives the request.
  5. The server checks your login details.
  6. The server sends your dashboard and course information.
  7. Your browser displays the webpage.

This entire process normally happens in just a few seconds.

docs.text:

docs.title: Challenge Activity
docs.text:

Explain why this statement is incorrect.

  • server
  • network

docs.title: Misconception 1
docs.text:
"The Internet stores my files."

Not exactly.

Your files are stored on servers connected to the Internet.

docs.title: Misconception 2
docs.text:
"Google is the Internet."

Google is a company that provides services on the Internet.

The Internet is the global network that connects millions of computers.

docs.title: Misconception 3
docs.text:
"DNS stores websites."

DNS does not store webpages.

It stores information that helps computers find the correct server.

docs.title: Misconception 4
docs.text:
"A server is always a huge machine."

Many servers are powerful computers in data centres, but a server is defined by its role—providing services—not by its physical size.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned that:

  • The Internet is a network of connected computers.
  • A client requests information.
  • A server provides information.
  • Every device needs an IP address.
  • Domain names make websites easier for people to remember.
  • DNS converts domain names into IP addresses.
  • Webpages are delivered through requests, responses and data packets.

docs.title: Vocabulary Review
docs.text: Word Meaning Client A device that requests information or services. Server A computer that provides information or services. IP Address A unique numerical address for a device on a network. Domain Name A human-readable website address. DNS The system that translates domain names into IP addresses. URL The address of a webpage or online resource. Packet A small piece of data sent across a network. Request A message asking for information. Response Information returned by a server.

docs.text:
When you type a website such as:

www.wikipedia.org

your computer cannot use that name directly.

}

docs.title: Key Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Protocol A set of rules that devices follow when communicating. TCP A protocol that ensures data is delivered correctly. IP A protocol used to identify devices and route data across networks. HTTP A protocol used to transfer web pages. HTTPS A secure version of HTTP that encrypts data. Packet A small piece of data sent across a network. Acknowledgement (ACK) A message confirming that data has been received. Encryption Converting data into a secure form so only authorised users can read it.

docs.title: Think About This
docs.text:
Imagine two people trying to play a board game.

The other person invents new rules whenever they want.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
• Would the game work?
  • Would it be fair?
  • Would both players understand what to do?

Now imagine millions of computers trying to communicate without agreed rules.

Would the Internet work?

docs.title: Why Do Computers Need Rules?
docs.text:
People communicate using languages and social rules.

For example:

  • We greet people politely.
  • We take turns speaking.
  • We listen before responding.

Computers also need rules.

These rules tell devices:

  • when to send data
  • where to send it
  • how to organise information
  • how to check for errors
  • what to do if information is lost

These communication rules are called network protocols.

docs.title: What Is a Network Protocol?
docs.text:
A network protocol is a set of agreed rules that allows computers and other devices to communicate.

Protocols define:

  • the format of messages
  • the order of communication
  • how errors are handled
  • how devices identify each other
  • how information is protected

Without protocols, devices would not understand one another.

docs.title: Everyday Analogy
docs.text:
Imagine sending a letter.

To arrive successfully, everyone follows agreed rules.

You must:

  1. Write the correct address.
  2. Place the letter in an envelope.
  3. Attach a stamp.
  4. Post it through the mail system.
  5. Wait for delivery.

Because everyone follows the same process, the letter reaches the correct destination.

The Internet works in a similar way.

Protocols provide the rules that every device follows.

docs.title: Classroom Example
docs.text:
Your teacher says:

"Write your name at the top of the page."

Everyone understands the instruction because everyone follows the same classroom rules.

Imagine if every student invented their own rule.

Some might write their name at the bottom.

Others might not write it at all.

Some could use symbols instead of letters.

The teacher would have difficulty identifying each student's work.

Computers face the same problem.

Protocols ensure every device communicates in the same way.

docs.title: Real-World Examples of Protocols
docs.text:
Protocols are used every day, even if you don't notice them.

Activity Protocol Example Visiting a website HTTP or HTTPS Sending an email SMTP Receiving an email IMAP or POP3 Streaming a video TCP/IP and HTTPS Browsing online DNS + HTTP/HTTPS + TCP/IP

Most online activities use several protocols working together.

docs.text: Now that you understand why protocols are necessary, the next section explains the most important protocol family on the Internet:

docs.title: TCP/IP
docs.text: These protocols make reliable communication between billions of devices possible.

docs.title: TCP/IP – The Language of the Internet
docs.text:
The Internet is not controlled by one computer or one company.

Instead, billions of devices communicate by following the same set of rules.

The most important collection of these rules is called the TCP/IP protocol suite.

TCP/IP makes it possible for devices made by different manufacturers, running different operating systems, to communicate successfully.

Without TCP/IP, the Internet as we know it would not exist.

docs.title: Two Important Protocols
docs.text:
Although TCP/IP includes many protocols, two are especially important.

Protocol Main Job IP (Internet Protocol) Finds the destination and routes data across networks. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) Ensures data arrives correctly and in the correct order.

Think of IP as choosing the route to a destination.

Think of TCP as checking that every package arrives safely.

docs.title: Understanding IP
docs.text:
IP is responsible for delivering data to the correct device.

Every device connected to a network has an IP address.

When you visit a website:

  1. DNS finds the website's IP address.
  2. Your computer creates data packets.
  3. IP decides where those packets should travel.
  4. Routers forward the packets toward the destination.

IP focuses on where data should go.

It does not guarantee that every packet will arrive.

docs.title: Understanding TCP
docs.text:
TCP works together with IP.

While IP delivers packets, TCP checks that communication is reliable.

TCP performs several important tasks:

  • divides large files into packets
  • numbers each packet
  • checks whether packets arrive
  • requests missing packets again
  • rebuilds the original message in the correct order

This makes Internet communication reliable even when networks are busy.

docs.title: Imagine Sending a Puzzle
docs.text:
Suppose you send a 500-piece jigsaw puzzle to a friend.

You place the pieces into several small boxes.

During delivery:

  • one box is delayed
  • another arrives first
  • one box is damaged

Without organisation, rebuilding the puzzle would be difficult.

TCP solves this problem.

It numbers every "box" (packet), checks that each one arrives, and requests another copy if one is missing.

docs.title: HTTP – Talking to Websites
docs.text:
When you open a website, your browser needs a way to communicate with the web server.

It uses HTTP, which stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol.

HTTP defines how:

  • browsers request web pages
  • servers send web pages
  • messages are organised
  • responses are returned

Without HTTP, web browsers would not know how to request webpages.

docs.title: A Simple HTTP Example
docs.text:
Your browser sends a request such as:

"Please send me the homepage."

The web server replies:

"Here is the webpage."

The browser then displays the page on your screen.

This conversation follows the rules of HTTP.

docs.title: HTTPS – A Safer Version of HTTP
docs.text:
Modern websites usually use HTTPS instead of HTTP.

The extra S stands for Secure.

HTTPS encrypts data before it is sent across the Internet.

Encryption protects information such as:

  • passwords
  • online banking details
  • shopping payments
  • personal messages

Whenever you see the padlock icon in your browser, HTTPS is helping to protect your connection.

docs.title: Why Is HTTPS Important?
docs.text:
Imagine sending a postcard.

Anyone handling the postcard can read the message.

Now imagine placing the message inside a locked envelope.

Only the intended recipient can read it.

HTTPS works like that locked envelope.

It helps protect information while it travels across the Internet.

docs.text:
HTTP HTTPS Transfers web pages Transfers web pages securely No encryption Uses encryption Less secure More secure Rarely used for sensitive information Used for banking, shopping and online accounts

Today, almost every major website uses HTTPS.

docs.title: How Protocols Work Together
docs.text:
When you visit a website, several protocols work together.

A simplified sequence is:

  1. Enter a web address.
  2. DNS finds the IP address.
  3. IP identifies the destination.
  4. TCP manages reliable delivery.
  5. HTTP or HTTPS transfers the webpage.
  6. Your browser displays the content.

Each protocol has a different job.

Together, they make web browsing possible.

docs.title: Key Idea
docs.text:
No single protocol runs the Internet.

Instead, many specialised protocols work together, with each one performing a different task.

This teamwork makes Internet communication fast, reliable and secure.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text:
So far, you have learned what each protocol does.

Next, you will discover how these protocols work together while data travels as packets across the network, and why acknowledgements (ACKs) make communication reliable.

docs.title: Packets and Acknowledgements (ACK)
docs.text:
When data travels across a network, it is divided into many small packets.

Each packet contains part of the original message.

After a packet reaches its destination, the receiving device sends back an Acknowledgement (ACK).

An ACK simply means:

"I received this packet successfully."

If an ACK is not received within a certain time, TCP assumes the packet was lost and sends it again.

This process helps ensure reliable communication.

docs.title: Example: Downloading a File
docs.text:
Imagine downloading a large photo.

The file is divided into many packets.

Packet 1 ✓
Packet 2 ✓
Packet 3 ✗ (Lost)
Packet 4 ✓
Packet 5 ✓

Because Packet 3 did not arrive, the receiving device does not send an ACK for it.

TCP requests Packet 3 again.

Once it arrives, the complete file can be reassembled correctly.

This all happens automatically, often in just a fraction of a second.

docs.title: Why Reliability Matters
docs.text:
Reliable communication is essential for many online activities.

Examples include:

  • online banking
  • submitting homework
  • sending emails
  • cloud storage
  • video conferencing
  • software updates

Imagine if part of a banking transaction or homework submission disappeared during transmission.

TCP helps prevent these kinds of problems.

Lab Overview
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will use Python to simulate how data travels across a network.

Instead of sending real network traffic, you will create a simple model of how protocols such as TCP organise information into packets.

By the end of this lab, you will understand how computers:

  • split data into packets
  • number packets
  • rebuild messages
  • detect missing packets

No networking libraries are required.

docs.title: Starter Activity
docs.text:
Imagine sending this message:

HELLO INTERNET

Would computers send it as one enormous block?

Usually not.

Instead, they divide the message into smaller pieces called packets.

Today, you will simulate this process.

docs.title: Activity 1 – Splitting a Message
docs.text:
Create a new Python file.

Type the following code.

message = "HELLO INTERNET"

packets = message.split()

print(packets)

Output

['HELLO', 'INTERNET']

The message has been divided into two simple packets.

docs.title: Activity 2 – Creating Numbered Packets
docs.text:
Real networks keep packets organised.

Let's number them.

message = "HELLO INTERNET"

words = message.split()

for number, packet in enumerate(words, start=1):
    print(number, packet)

Output

1 HELLO
2 INTERNET

Each packet now has a sequence number.

This helps TCP rebuild information correctly.

docs.title: Understanding enumerate()
docs.text:
The function

enumerate()

adds numbers to items in a list.

Example

animals = ["cat", "dog", "bird"]

for number, animal in enumerate(animals, start=1):
    print(number, animal)

Output

1 cat
2 dog
3 bird

This idea is similar to numbering packets in a network.

docs.title: Activity 3 – Building Packet Objects
docs.text:
Instead of storing only words, store additional information.

message = "HELLO INTERNET"

packets = []

for number, word in enumerate(message.split(), start=1):

    packet = {
        "number": number,
        "data": word
    }

    packets.append(packet)

print(packets)

Output

[
 {'number': 1, 'data': 'HELLO'},
 {'number': 2, 'data': 'INTERNET'}
]

Each packet now stores:

  • a packet number
  • the packet contents

docs.title: Activity 4 – Displaying Packets
docs.text:
Loop through the packets.

for packet in packets:
    print(packet["number"], packet["data"])

Output

1 HELLO
2 INTERNET

This is much easier to read.

docs.title: Activity 5 – Rebuilding the Message
docs.text:
Suppose all packets arrive safely.

We can rebuild the original message.

message = ""

for packet in packets:
    message += packet["data"] + " "

print(message)

Output

HELLO INTERNET

The receiver has reconstructed the original message.

docs.title: But what happens if one packet disappears?
Activity 6 – Simulating Packet Loss
docs.text:
In real networks, packets do not always arrive successfully.

Let's simulate a missing packet.

packets = [
    {"number": 1, "data": "HELLO"},
    {"number": 2, "data": "INTERNET"},
    {"number": 3, "data": "CLASS"}
]

# Simulate packet loss
del packets[1]

print(packets)

Output

[
 {'number': 1, 'data': 'HELLO'},
 {'number': 3, 'data': 'CLASS'}
]

Packet 2 has disappeared.

docs.title: Why Is This a Problem?
docs.text:
Try rebuilding the message.

message = ""

for packet in packets:
    message += packet["data"] + " "

print(message)

Output

HELLO CLASS

The word INTERNET is missing.

This is why reliable communication is important.

docs.title: Activity 7 – Detecting Missing Packets
docs.text:
We can check whether every packet number is present.

expected = [1, 2, 3]

received = []

for packet in packets:
    received.append(packet["number"])

for number in expected:
    if number not in received:
        print("Missing packet:", number)

Output

Missing packet: 2

This is similar to what TCP does before rebuilding a message.

docs.title: Activity 8 – Simulating an ACK
docs.text:
When a packet arrives successfully, the receiver sends an acknowledgement.

packets = [
    {"number": 1, "data": "HELLO"},
    {"number": 2, "data": "INTERNET"},
    {"number": 3, "data": "CLASS"}
]

for packet in packets:
    print(f"Packet {packet['number']} received.")
    print(f"ACK {packet['number']} sent.\n")

Output

Packet 1 received.
ACK 1 sent.

Packet 2 received.
ACK 2 sent.

Packet 3 received.
ACK 3 sent.

In real networks, ACK messages tell the sender that packets arrived successfully.

docs.title: Activity 9 – Retransmitting a Missing Packet
docs.text:
Imagine packet 2 was lost.

The sender sends it again.

received = [1, 3]

if 2 not in received:
    print("Packet 2 missing.")
    print("Resending packet 2...")

Output

Packet 2 missing.
Resending packet 2...

This simple simulation demonstrates one of TCP's key features.

docs.title: Activity 10 – Reordering Packets
docs.text:
Packets do not always arrive in order.

packets = [
    {"number": 3, "data": "CLASS"},
    {"number": 1, "data": "HELLO"},
    {"number": 2, "data": "INTERNET"}
]

Sort them before rebuilding.

packets.sort(key=lambda packet: packet["number"])

for packet in packets:
    print(packet)

Output

{'number': 1, 'data': 'HELLO'}
{'number': 2, 'data': 'INTERNET'}
{'number': 3, 'data': 'CLASS'}

TCP performs a similar task when packets arrive out of order.

docs.title: What is Cybersecurity?
docs.text:
Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks, programs, and data from attacks or unauthorised access.

Examples include:

  • Unlocking a phone with biometrics
  • Shopping online
  • Internet banking
  • Secure messaging
  • School accounts

docs.title: Why Does Cybersecurity Matter?
docs.text:
Without cybersecurity, attackers may:

  • Steal personal information
  • Delete files
  • Spread malware
  • Lock computers with ransomware
  • Steal money

docs.title: The CIA Triad
docs.text: Principle Meaning Confidentiality Only authorised users can access data. Integrity Data cannot be changed without permission. Availability Data is available when needed.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
For a school grading system:

  • Confidentiality → Only teachers can view grades.
  • Integrity → Students cannot change grades.
  • Availability → Teachers can access grades when needed.

docs.text:

  • Strong passwords
  • Multi-factor authentication
  • Antivirus software
  • Firewalls
  • Software updates
  • HTTPS websites

docs.title: Introduction

Computer networks continue to evolve. New technologies allow devices to communicate faster, smarter, and more securely than ever before.

docs.title: Cloud Computing
docs.text:
Cloud computing allows users to store files and run applications on remote servers instead of a local computer.

Examples include: - Google Drive - Microsoft OneDrive - Dropbox

Benefits: - Access files anywhere - Automatic backups - Easy collaboration - Reduced hardware costs

docs.title: Internet of Things (IoT)
docs.text:
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical devices connected to the Internet.

Examples: - Smart watches - Smart lights - Smart speakers - Smart home security cameras

IoT devices collect and share data automatically.

docs.title: Edge Computing
docs.text:
Instead of sending all data to distant cloud servers, edge computing processes some data close to where it is created.

Benefits: - Faster response time - Lower network traffic - Better performance for real-time applications

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence in Networks
docs.text: AI can help manage computer networks by: - Detecting cyber attacks - Predicting equipment failures - Optimising network traffic - Improving security

docs.title: 5G Networks
docs.text:

Applications include autonomous vehicles, smart factories and remote healthcare.
